source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 35% of people in Ireland were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
23.4% of health spending in Ireland was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
2.9% of people in Ireland reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
22% of hospital care costs in Ireland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
20% of outpatient medical care costs in Ireland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
71% of dental care costs in Ireland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
21% of pharmaceutical costs in Ireland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.

In Ireland, although coverage is universal, fewer than half of the population are covered for the cost of all general practitioner (GP) services, but new eligibility measures introduced since 2023 have increased the proportion covered.
Duplicate private health insurance was most widely used in Australia and Ireland.
This is especially notable in Finland, Lithuania, Ireland, Greece, Spain and France, where unmet medical care needs due to waiting times increased by 1.4 percentage points or more since 2019.
The most generous coverage was found in France (83%), Germany (82%) and Ireland (79%).

This varies considerably across OECD countries, from fewer than 2% of households experiencing catastrophic health spending in Sweden, Slovenia, the United Kingdom, Ireland and the Netherlands, to over 10% of households in Lithuania, Latvia and Hungary (Figure 5.10).
Data come mainly from administrative sources, although in some countries (including Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand and Switzerland) they come from health interview surveys.
Remote consultations cannot be distinguished and are included in a few countries (such as Austria from 2020, and Ireland, Japan, Latvia, the Netherlands, the Slovak Republic and Spain from 2019).

This covers a wide range of facilities with most spending related to either medical practices including GPs and specialists (as in Austria, France and Germany) or ambulatory healthcare centres (as in Finland, Ireland and Sweden).
As a result, day care services account for 15% or more of all hospital expenditures in Belgium, Ireland and Portugal.
